extracted.intended_audience: comic artists and illustrators (beginner to intermediate) learning composition and visual storytelling
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and concrete principles for composing single illustrations and comic panels/pages to direct viewer attention, control flow, and elicit intended emotional responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition (overall)
rubrics_metrics.description: Composition is the ART of arranging and presenting your ART — a skill about how to combine several elements in a visual way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Composition is never just one element; it is the mix of many fundamentals (anatomy, shading, perspective, line quality, etc.) and how they are distributed on the page. Good composition boosts the collective impact of all fundamentals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus
rubrics_metrics.description: Where you want the viewer to look.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common focuses: Action (for comics), character faces, major props, and Story Points. Always make the story point clear — without it you're just drawing figures. Panels/illustrations often have multiple focal points with varying priorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Directing focus — Lines
rubrics_metrics.description: Use objects' contours and line-work to 'point toward' where you want the viewer to look.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intentionally orient line-work so it points back toward the chosen focus (e.g., a character's face). Contour/gesture lines can lead the eye between focal points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Directing focus — Detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Add more detail, crisper lines, and rendering where you want attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Areas with higher detail/texture (e.g., cross-hatching) attract the eye; use rendering to emphasize higher-priority focal points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Directing focus — Value (contrast)
rubrics_metrics.description: Contrast of light and shadow is the strongest way to direct focus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High contrast areas draw the eye first. Use values intentionally to establish and support focal hierarchy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Directing focus — Saturation (for color work)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use color saturation to make focal points stand out in colored illustrations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Boost saturation at the focal point as a secondary tool when coloring to immediately attract attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fibonacci / Rule of Thirds (Golden Ratio)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the Golden Ratio / Rule of Thirds to divide the frame and place elements where they are visually appealing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place important objects at grid intersections and use the ratio (2/3 vs 1/3) to create asymmetrical dynamic relationships — one element dominates (2/3) while another supports (1/3). Apply the ratio to questions of 'how much?' (detail, color, number of elements).

rubrics_metrics.name: Silver Ratio
rubrics_metrics.description: An alternative grid dividing the frame into halves and quarters to create a more 'forced' or interesting look.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aligning elements to halfway and quarter marks can produce an unnatural but compelling effect; useful when you want a different visual tension than the Golden Ratio.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flow (story, page, panel)
rubrics_metrics.description: How elements piece together to lead the viewer through the story, page, or single panel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of story flow (across pages), page flow (how panels and word bubbles guide reading), and panel flow (single-shot composition). Maintain a single line of action/flow for shots; avoid elements that interrupt the eye-path.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use shapes to establish flow
rubrics_metrics.description: Start with foundational shapes (diamonds, squares, triangles, circles) to create inherent motion and flow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a chosen shape as a compositional guide for gestures and layout (e.g., circular flow for a running figure). Sync character gestures with background/secondary elements to maintain consistent flow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish focal priorities before drawing
rubrics_metrics.description: Write down a few bullet-point focal priorities in order of importance before beginning the drawing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List priorities (e.g., 'Protagonist — Courageous; Monolith — Legendary; Journey — more to traverse') and pair each with a specific technique to realize it. This helps maintain intention during sketching and refinement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feel — Orientation
rubrics_metrics.description: Orientation of shapes (horizontal/vertical/diagonal) influences emotional tone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Horizontal = calm/still; Vertical = energized/resisting gravity; Diagonal = instability/motion. Use panel and composition orientation to reinforce mood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feel — Location in frame
rubrics_metrics.description: Placement of objects within the frame conveys importance and motion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 'Almost off-frame' implies transit/less importance; Centered shows high importance; Bottom = grounded/ordinary; Upper = extraordinary/powerful. Use placement to support narrative emphasis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feel — Shape language
rubrics_metrics.description: Pointed vs round shapes carry implicit emotional meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pointed shapes feel dangerous/threatening; round shapes feel safe/friendly. Apply shape language to character and environment design (e.g., make villains pointy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Feel — Size within the frame (scale and dominance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Relative size of objects in the frame determines perceived importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Larger objects feel more important; placing a character closer to the camera increases dominance. Equal sizes imply equal story value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feel — Shape vs Color perceptual priority
rubrics_metrics.description: Humans differentiate colors faster than shapes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if shapes are similar, differing colors will be noticed first. Use color strategically when you need quick visual distinction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feel — Scale, location and perceived distance (perspective/fear)
rubrics_metrics.description: Relative scale and overlap create depth and influence emotional reactions (e.g., fear of approaching danger).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Smaller repeating shapes imply distance/perspective; overlapping objects indicate closeness. Use scale and placement to manipulate tension (fear of the unknown vs immediate threat).

rubrics_metrics.name: Depth and separation (silhouettes, line weight, overlapping, value)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use silhouette clarity, varied line weight, overlapping shapes, and value differences to separate foreground, midground, and background.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thicker line weights in foreground push background farther away; silhouettes maintain readable shapes; overlapping and value shifts convey depth and distance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical workflow: iterate from comp to refinement
rubrics_metrics.description: Start with rough composition and shapes, assess focus/flow/feel, then refine line work and adjust composition to push focal points and feeling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't over-refine early; re-center on composition through multiple passes (thumbnail → rough sketch → refined line). Adjust elements (shape, line weight, value, detail) in later passes to better realize compositional intent.
